title: coldstart-throughput-degradation-smokeplan
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures an operational smoke-test and troubleshooting playbook focused on a recurring failure class we saw during Private (VPC / on-prem) upgrades: a significant cold-start throughput regression after a control-plane or runtime change. The goal is to give on-call and rollout engineers a compact, reproducible checklist, diagnostic commands, terraform-module cautions, and a safe canary upgrade recipe.

When to use this doc:
- After any runtime or kernel/CUDA/driver upgrade for a Private deployment.
- When customer reports increased per-request latency on first-hit traffic or low concurrency throughput for new processes after deploy.
- During canary rollouts when metrics show widened p95/p99 startup latency.

Quick TL;DR summary:
- Run the quick smoke bundle (Section: Smoke-test checklist). If failures seen, run targeted diagnostics (Network, Container runtime, Kernel resources, GPU driver mismatch).
- Common root causes we repeatedly see: MTU mismatch across nodes and LB, iptables DROP rules silently throttling SYNs, containerd vs dockerd OCI runtime mis-config, missing hugepages or wrong vm.max_map_count, CUDA driver + runtime ABI mismatch, slow NFS/backing store mounts causing process init timeouts.
- Mitigation: stage rollback, pin Terraform module/provider versions, fix MTU and iptables then re-run smoke tests; if driver mismatch, roll back to previous runtime image.

Pre-upgrade Terraform checks (do these every time):
1) terraform init && terraform validate in a fresh workspace.
2) terraform plan -out=plan.bin -var-file=env.prod.tfvars | tee plan.txt; scan plan.txt for "-/+ replace" or resources to be recreated that touch network interfaces or load-balancers.
3) Ensure remote state lock is working (state backend health). Run: terraform state pull | head -n 40.
4) Provider pinning: confirm provider versions in required_providers block. Do not accept provider upgrades as part of a patch upgrade unless validated.
5) Check for manual taints: terraform state list | grep module.node && terraform state show <resource> to confirm no stale IPs.
6) If using bootstrap modules that insert iptables rules, grep module source for "provisioner" blocks that run scripts on instance launch — these are frequently the source of MTU/iptables drift.

Terraform module notes / common pitfalls:
- Module variable allow_drift: default false in our modules; accidentally setting true during automated upgrades allowed ephemeral changes that broke MTU. Keep false until after smoke-tests pass.
- Don't replace network interfaces in-place if you cannot coordinate LB and routes; if Terraform wants to replace, prefer a manual canary node first.
- Keep a small script to compare instance network settings after apply: ssh to canary && sudo ip -d link show | grep mtu
- Always run terraform apply with -refresh=true and capture the plan output. Save plan artifacts in build artifacts to allow diffs vs previous.

Smoke-test checklist (quick bundle) — run this immediately after a canary node finishes init and reconverges:
1) Basic API OK: curl -sS -w "%{http_code}\nTime:%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null https://<canary-ip>/v1/health => expect 200 and time_total < 0.25s for HTTPS LB local network.
2) 5 concurrent small generation (50 tokens) with default model: run the smoke script (bin/smoke-gen --concurrency 5 --tokens 50). Success criteria: 5/5 responses, no 5xx, median latency < 300ms, p95 < 800ms.
3) Embedding runner: run 20 embedding requests in a tight loop and confirm fewer than 5% errors and consistent vector norms (basic normalization check).
4) KV cache warmup: send a repeated prompt sequence X3 and verify the second and third call have >10% lower latency (prefix/KV caching).
5) Batch path: issue a small 16-concurrency batch to validate batching code path. Throughput should increase vs single-run.
6) GPU health: nvidia-smi (or rocm-smi) shows expected GPUs online, driver version matches expected release. Look for "No running processes found" only if idle; otherwise GPU memory and compute should register during the smoke runs.
7) Disk and mount checks: df -h and lsblk to ensure expected mountpoints (modelstore) are present and not "stale NFS".
8) DNS: dig +short internal-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local should resolve within <20ms.

If any of the above fail, escalate to targeted diagnostics below.

Targeted diagnostics by failure signature:
A) Symptom: First-request latency very high then subsequent requests fast (cold-start only).
- Check: dmesg | grep -i hugepage OR grep -i transparent_hugepage; check /proc/meminfo HugePages_Free. Also check vm.max_map_count and sysctl vm.nr_hugepages.
- Remediation: enable static hugepages (or increase vm.nr_hugepages) and tune container runtime settings. If using Java-based subprocesses in runtime, increase vm.max_map_count.

B) Symptom: All requests slow, connection setup appears slow, large number of retransmits
- Check: sudo ss -s; sudo ip -s link show dev eth0; sudo ethtool -S eth0; sudo iptables -L -n -v | grep DROP
- Look for MTU mismatches: ip -d link show | grep mtu and compare across nodes + LB. If MTU mismatch detected (e.g., 1500 vs 9000), set correct MTU or enable path MTU probing (sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1) as short-term mitigation.
- Check for iptables rules injected by cloud-init/user-data scripts. If we see DROP counters on expected ports, revert those rules and re-run smoke.

C) Symptom: GPU memory allocation errors, model load fails after upgrade
- Check: journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200 | grep -i cuda
- Run: nvidia-smi -q | grep -i 'Driver Version' and compare to expected in release notes. Also check libcuda.so ABI: strings /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so | head -n 5
- Remediation: roll back driver or runtime image to one with matching CUDA ABI or coordinate driver upgrade across nodes.

D) Symptom: Processes stuck in init, high page-faults, slow file opens
- Check: pidstat -r -p <pid> 1 5; perf top (if available) to locate syscall hotspots; strace -f -p <pid> for blocked syscalls.
- Frequent cause: slow NFS/remote modelstore. Check mount stats: cat /proc/mounts | grep modelstore and stat -f /path 
- Remediation: fallback to local cache copies, mark node as degraded and remove from rotation until NFS healthy.

Useful diagnostic commands (copy-paste friendly):
- systemctl status redwood-runtime.service --no-pager
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since "15 minutes ago" -n 300 | sed -n '1,400p'
- docker ps -a || crictl ps -a
- crictl inspect <container-id> | jq .state
- ip -d link show dev eth0; ethtool -k eth0; ss -tunlp | grep :443
- sudo iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers | sed -n '1,200p'
- sudo cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_mtu_probing
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,memory.total --format=csv
- df -h /var/lib/redwood-models; mount | grep modelstore

Rollout / canary upgrade recipe (safe default):
1) Lock autoscaler and freeze any horizontal scaling for the cluster to avoid noisy replaces.
2) Choose 1-2 canary nodes in a single rack/zone to limit blast radius.
3) Apply terraform only for the canary subset: use targeting (careful) or run the instance replace manually.
4) Wait for node to pass node-level init hooks (cloud-init logs clean).
5) Run full smoke-test bundle (above). If failure, collect all logs, capture core dumps, run diagnostics and stop rollout.
6) If smoke passes, expand to 10% nodes, run subset smoke-tests, watch metrics for 30-60 minutes.
7) If stable, proceed linear rollout with 20% increments and 1 hour hold per batch.
8) If at any stage p95 startup latency jumps > 2x baseline or > 500ms absolute, abort and roll back nodes replaced in last batch.

Rollback guidance:
- Keep previous machine image and runtime image pinned. If rollback is needed, re-image replaced nodes rather than attempting in-place revert of kernel/driver changes.
- For Terraform-induced network replacements, sometimes the fastest path is to restore previous state file to a temporary workspace and run a targeted apply for the affected network resources, then re-run smoke.

Post-incident capture checklist (what to collect before tearing down):
- tar.gz of /var/log/redwood-runtime, journalctl -u redwood-runtime logs, dmesg, output of nvidia-smi -q, output of ip -d link show and iptables -L -n -v, mount output and df -h.
- Copy of terraform plan (plan.txt) and terraform state snapshot.
- Flamegraph or pprof from the runtime if available.
- Rule of thumb: store all artifacts under s3://redwood-pd-debug/<incident-id>/ with 90-day retention.

Example failure signatures to grep for (quick):
- grep -E "(CUDA_ERROR|failed to initialize GPU|unsatisfied link|segfault)" /var/log/redwood-runtime/*.log
- grep -E "(connection timed out|connection reset|SYN_RECV|retransmit)" /var/log/syslog /var/log/messages
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime | grep -i "oom\|segfault\|libcuda\|tensor"

Notes and follow-ups for infra team (longer-term fixes):
- Add a post-terraform check to automatically capture MTU and iptables counters for any node whose interfaces were modified. Make that a gating check in our CD pipeline.
- Improve module test coverage for provider upgrades: run a staged lab that applies the module against multiple image/driver combinations.
- Add a lightweight canary agent that runs smoke-bundle automatically and uploads results to the rollout dashboard (automate step 5).

Appendix: quick checklist you can print in a paging situation:
- Verify terraform plan for network changes (do not apply blindly).
- Run smoke-bundle on canary node.
- If cold-start only: check hugepages & vm.max_map_count.
- If all requests slow: check MTU, iptables, path MTU probing.
- If GPU errors: check driver and ABI match.
- If NFS-related stalls: check mount health and fallback to local cache.
- Collect logs (redwood-runtime, systemd, dmesg, iptables, nvidia-smi).

Contact matrix (quick):
- Infra (network/terraform): Michael Chen
- Serving runtime: Ravi Kapoor
- Release / Canary owner: Leah Ortiz

This document is intentionally concise and operational. Save any post-mortem details and long analysis to the incident page linked above. If this playbook blocks you during a live incident, escalate to the contacts above and attach the artifact bundle before making a rollback decision.
